title: Cyber Threat Intelligence: The Discipline
description: Cyber threat intelligence turns scattered indicators, hashes, IPs, tactics, into actionable knowledge about adversaries. The intelligence cycle, direction, collection, processing, analysis, dissemination, is the same tradecraft intelligence agencies have used for a century, applied to networks.
content:
Cyber threat intelligence turns scattered indicators, hashes, IPs, tactics, into actionable knowledge about adversaries. The intelligence cycle, direction, collection, processing, analysis, dissemination, is the same tradecraft intelligence agencies have used for a century, applied to networks.

Maturity is measured by use: low-maturity teams collect feeds, high-maturity teams drive hunting and architecture from finished intelligence. The public frameworks, MITRE ATT&CK, the Cyber Kill Chain, give everyone the same map.

It is a young discipline with old roots, and its best practitioners think like analysts first and technologists second.
key_facts: Indicators to knowledge via the intelligence cycle
MITRE ATT&CK and Kill Chain: the public maps
Maturity measured by operational use
Analysts first, technologists second

title: OSINT: Open-Source Intelligence Methods
description: OSINT collects intelligence from public sources: DNS records, certificate logs, code repositories, social media, and leaked datasets. The methods are legal by definition, they use only what is published, and their power comes from correlation across sources.
content:
OSINT collects intelligence from public sources: DNS records, certificate logs, code repositories, social media, and leaked datasets. The methods are legal by definition, they use only what is published, and their power comes from correlation across sources.

The discipline's ethics are consent and minimization: public does not mean harmless to aggregate, and professional OSINT respects that boundary. Certificate Transparency logs alone map much of the internet's infrastructure.

Done well, OSINT answers questions without touching the target at all.
key_facts: Public sources only: DNS, certs, repos, leaks
Power from correlation across sources
Ethics: consent and minimization
Answers questions without touching targets

title: Security Operations Centers
description: A SOC watches the network around the clock: tier-1 analysts triage alerts, tier-2 investigates, tier-3 hunts proactively. The SIEM aggregates logs; the SOAR platform automates the repetitive responses.
content:
A SOC watches the network around the clock: tier-1 analysts triage alerts, tier-2 investigates, tier-3 hunts proactively. The SIEM aggregates logs; the SOAR platform automates the repetitive responses.

The industry's pain is alert fatigue: thousands of daily alerts, most false positives, tuned by detection engineering. Good SOCs measure mean time to detect and respond, and improve both relentlessly.

The SOC is where intelligence becomes action, or dies in a queue.
key_facts: Tiered analysts: triage, investigate, hunt
SIEM aggregates; SOAR automates responses
Alert fatigue is the industry pain
MTTD and MTTR are the vital metrics

title: Indicators of Compromise
description: IOCs are the forensic artifacts of intrusion: file hashes, IPs, domains, registry keys, and behavioral patterns. They are shared in STIX/TAXII feeds so one victim's discovery protects everyone else.
content:
IOCs are the forensic artifacts of intrusion: file hashes, IPs, domains, registry keys, and behavioral patterns. They are shared in STIX/TAXII feeds so one victim's discovery protects everyone else.

IOCs decay: attackers rotate infrastructure in hours, so freshness determines value. Behavior-based indicators, TTPs, outlive atomic ones, which is why ATT&CK mapping matters more than hash lists.

Sharing is the defense: the feed economy is collective immunity.
key_facts: Hashes, IPs, domains, behaviors: intrusion artifacts
STIX/TAXII: the sharing formats
IOCs decay in hours; TTPs outlive them
Sharing is collective immunity

title: Cyber-Espionage: Public Cases
description: Public cyber-espionage cases, from Titan Rain to the OPM breach to SolarWinds, are documented in indictments, reports, and hearings. The pattern is persistent access for collection, not destruction, and dwell times measured in months.
content:
Public cyber-espionage cases, from Titan Rain to the OPM breach to SolarWinds, are documented in indictments, reports, and hearings. The pattern is persistent access for collection, not destruction, and dwell times measured in months.

The public lesson is architectural: assume breach, segment networks, and monitor east-west traffic, because perimeter defense failed in every major case. Zero trust is the doctrine that resulted.

History here is a curriculum, and it is all public.
key_facts: Titan Rain, OPM, SolarWinds: documented public cases
Pattern: persistent collection, months of dwell
Lesson: assume breach, segment, monitor laterally
Zero trust is the resulting doctrine

title: Critical Infrastructure Protection
description: Power grids, water systems, and hospitals are protected as national priorities: NERC CIP standards mandate controls for the bulk power system, and CISA coordinates public-private defense. The 2021 Colonial Pipeline incident showed the cascading stakes.
content:
Power grids, water systems, and hospitals are protected as national priorities: NERC CIP standards mandate controls for the bulk power system, and CISA coordinates public-private defense. The 2021 Colonial Pipeline incident showed the cascading stakes.

OT security differs from IT: availability outranks confidentiality, patching windows are measured in years, and safety systems must never be reachable from the network. Air gaps are policy; unidirectional gateways are engineering.

Protection here is civil defense for the digital age.
key_facts: NERC CIP, CISA coordination: the public framework
Colonial Pipeline (2021): the cascading stakes
OT priorities: availability over confidentiality
Air gaps as policy; gateways as engineering

title: Cyber Ranges: Training Grounds
description: Cyber ranges are simulated networks where defenders practice against live red teams: full enterprise replicas with traffic, users, and vulnerabilities. National exercises like Cyber Storm test coordination at scale.
content:
Cyber ranges are simulated networks where defenders practice against live red teams: full enterprise replicas with traffic, users, and vulnerabilities. National exercises like Cyber Storm test coordination at scale.

The training value is muscle memory: incident response learned in simulation transfers to real breaches. Ranges also validate tools and playbooks before production.

Rehearsal is the difference between a plan and a capability.

Red team versus blue team with real traffic
Cyber Storm: national coordination exercises

title: AI in Cybersecurity: Public State
description: AI serves defense in detection, triage, and hunting: anomaly detection on logs, phishing classification, and malware-family clustering. Attackers use the same tools for polymorphism and social engineering at scale.
content:
AI serves defense in detection, triage, and hunting: anomaly detection on logs, phishing classification, and malware-family clustering. Attackers use the same tools for polymorphism and social engineering at scale.

The honest assessment is augmentation, not autonomy: AI cuts analyst workload but still needs human judgment for novel tradecraft. Adversarial ML, attacks on the detectors themselves, is the field's open flank.

The race is symmetric; the advantage goes to whoever evaluates more rigorously.
key_facts: Detection, triage, hunting: the defensive uses
Attackers use the same tools in reverse
Augmentation, not autonomy, is the honest state
Adversarial ML is the open flank

title: Information Sharing: CISA and ISACs
description: CISA coordinates US federal civilian cybersecurity, and ISACs share threat data within sectors, finance, health, energy. The legal framework, including liability protections, exists to make sharing safe.
content:
CISA coordinates US federal civilian cybersecurity, and ISACs share threat data within sectors, finance, health, energy. The legal framework, including liability protections, exists to make sharing safe.

Sharing works when it is automated and anonymized: machine-readable indicators flow in minutes, and analysts add context. Trust is the infrastructure, built through consistent contribution.

Collective defense is the only defense that scales with the threat.

ISACs share within sectors under liability protections
Automated, anonymated, machine-readable flows

title: Digital Forensics Fundamentals
description: Digital forensics recovers the story from disk images, memory dumps, and logs: file carving, timeline analysis, and artifact parsing, all under chain-of-custody discipline. The methods are courtroom-tested.
content:
Digital forensics recovers the story from disk images, memory dumps, and logs: file carving, timeline analysis, and artifact parsing, all under chain-of-custody discipline. The methods are courtroom-tested.

Memory forensics catches what disk misses: injected code, network connections, and encryption keys live in RAM. Volatility and its successors are public tools.

Forensics is archaeology with legal standards: every claim must survive cross-examination.
key_facts: Disk, memory, and log analysis under chain of custody
Memory forensics catches injected code and keys
Volatility: the public toolkit
Courtroom-tested methods

title: Network Architecture for Defense
description: Defensible networks are segmented: trust zones, DMZs, and microsegmentation limit lateral movement so one compromised host does not mean a compromised enterprise. The design principle is least privilege applied to packets.
content:
Defensible networks are segmented: trust zones, DMZs, and microsegmentation limit lateral movement so one compromised host does not mean a compromised enterprise. The design principle is least privilege applied to packets.

Visibility is the companion: NetFlow, DNS logs, and TLS metadata reveal behavior without breaking encryption. Architecture that cannot be monitored cannot be defended.

Segmentation plus visibility is the oldest advice and still the best.
key_facts: Segmentation limits lateral movement
Zones, DMZs, microsegmentation: the layers
NetFlow, DNS, TLS metadata: monitorable without decryption
Least privilege applied to packets

title: Zero-Trust Architecture
description: Zero trust assumes no implicit trust from network location: every access is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted, continuously. NIST SP 800-207 is the public reference architecture.
content:
Zero trust assumes no implicit trust from network location: every access is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted, continuously. NIST SP 800-207 is the public reference architecture.

The pillars are identity, device health, and least-privilege access, with policy engines deciding per request. Microsegmentation and software-defined perimeters are the enforcement.

It is a strategy, not a product, despite what vendors claim.
key_facts: Never trust, always verify: no implicit network trust
NIST SP 800-207: the reference architecture
Identity, device health, least privilege: the pillars
A strategy, not a product

title: Encryption Standards: Public Bedrock
description: AES-256 and ChaCha20 encrypt the world's data; RSA and elliptic curves handle key exchange; SHA-2 and SHA-3 provide integrity. All are public, standardized, and battle-tested by decades of cryptanalysis.
content:
AES-256 and ChaCha20 encrypt the world's data; RSA and elliptic curves handle key exchange; SHA-2 and SHA-3 provide integrity. All are public, standardized, and battle-tested by decades of cryptanalysis.

Post-quantum migration is underway: NIST's selected algorithms, Kyber for key exchange and Dilithium for signatures, are being deployed before quantum computers break the old ones. 'Harvest now, decrypt later' drives the urgency.

Open standards plus open cryptanalysis is why the bedrock holds.
key_facts: AES-256, ChaCha20: symmetric workhorses
RSA/ECC for exchange; SHA-2/3 for integrity
Post-quantum: Kyber and Dilithium deploying now
Open analysis is the security argument

title: Incident Response: The Playbook
description: Incident response follows the cycle: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. Tabletop exercises rehearse it; retainers guarantee expert help when minutes matter.
content:
Incident response follows the cycle: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. Tabletop exercises rehearse it; retainers guarantee expert help when minutes matter.

Containment decisions are business decisions: isolating a revenue system costs money, and the playbook pre-authorizes the tradeoffs. Communication plans cover customers, regulators, and law enforcement.

The postmortem is the product: every incident must improve the defenses, or the pain was wasted.

Containment is a pre-authorized business decision
Communication covers customers, regulators, police

title: Public-Private Partnerships
description: Cybersecurity is inherently partnered: most infrastructure is private, most intelligence starts classified, and defense needs both. JCDC and similar bodies plan jointly; exercises rehearse the partnership.
content:
Cybersecurity is inherently partnered: most infrastructure is private, most intelligence starts classified, and defense needs both. JCDC and similar bodies plan jointly; exercises rehearse the partnership.

The friction points are classification, liability, and speed, and the public record shows steady work on each. Partnerships succeed on shared operations, not shared slogans.

No single organization defends alone; the partnership is the perimeter.
key_facts: Most infrastructure private; much intel starts classified
JCDC: joint planning body
Friction: classification, liability, speed
Shared operations over shared slogans

title: Cyber Hygiene: The Fundamentals
description: The fundamentals stop most attacks: patched software, multi-factor authentication, backups, least privilege, and phishing-resistant habits. The UK's Cyber Essentials and CISA's guidance say the same things because they work.
content:
The fundamentals stop most attacks: patched software, multi-factor authentication, backups, least privilege, and phishing-resistant habits. The UK's Cyber Essentials and CISA's guidance say the same things because they work.

Hygiene is unglamorous and decisive: the majority of breaches exploit known vulnerabilities and missing MFA. Basics done consistently beat advanced tools done sporadically.

Every advanced program in this database assumes these are already in place.

Most breaches exploit known issues and missing MFA
Consistent basics beat sporadic advanced tools
The foundation every program assumes
